content: Viral gastroenteritis refers to the inflammation of the stomach, small intestine, and large intestine caused by various viruses. This condition often leads to symptoms such as vomiting and diarrhea. Despite being commonly referred to as the stomach flu, it is not caused by influenza viruses. A range of viruses can cause viral gastroenteritis, including rotaviruses, noroviruses, adenovirus types 40 and 41, sapoviruses, and astroviruses. It is important to note that this condition is not caused by bacteria (e.g., Salmonella or Escherichia coli), parasites (e.g., Giardia), medications, or other medical conditions, even though the symptoms may appear similar. Rotavirus infections can be diagnosed through laboratory testing of stool samples. While routine testing for other viruses that cause gastroenteritis is not commonly performed, specialized analysis can be conducted by the viral gastroenteritis unit at the CDC upon request. The primary focus of treatment for viral gastroenteritis, particularly in children and adults, is the prevention of dehydration. This management should ideally begin at home. Physicians may provide specific guidance on the types of fluids to administer. The CDC advises families with infants and young children to keep a supply of oral rehydration solution (ORS) at home and to use it as soon as diarrhea begins. Medications, including antibiotics (which are ineffective against viruses) and other treatments, should only be used if explicitly recommended by a healthcare provider. Currently, a licensed rotavirus vaccine is available to protect infants and young children from severe diarrhea caused by rotavirus infection. Research is ongoing to develop a vaccine for norovirus. Preventive measures include frequent handwashing, prompt disinfection of contaminated surfaces using household chlorine bleach-based cleaners, and immediate washing of soiled clothing. If food or water is suspected to be contaminated, it should be avoided.
